data.title: Probe A — results
body: # Probe A — results
- **Date carried out:** 2026-09-02
- **Hypothesis:** conflicts when merging tasks are a pain teams feel in practice (assumption #1, Risk 8.0)
- **Data:** [probe-a-data.csv](probe-a-data.csv)
## Method
Backlog.md and git-issues tasks are files in git, so the history of their merges is available to read. Instead of asking people whether conflicts happen, we **counted** them.
1. Through GitHub code search, 245 public repositories with `backlog/tasks/` or `.issues/` were found.
2. Each was cloned partially (`--filter=blob:none --no-checkout`).

3. **Every merge commit was reproduced anew** through `git merge-tree --write-tree` on its two parents. Git itself reports whether a conflict arose — this is not a heuristic but the same mechanism that runs on a real merge.
4. Conflicts were filtered by the path to the task files.

**Why not `git show --cc`.** The first attempt used the combined diff, and it produced false positives: `--cc` shows files created in the merge commit itself as something that "differs from both parents". Reproducing the merge does not have that flaw.
## Results
| Measure | Value |
| Candidates found | 245 |
| Filtered out: no task files | 42 |
| Filtered out: no merge commits | 73 |
| **Suitable for analysis** | **130** |
| **Merge commits reproduced** | **8,396** |
| With a conflict anywhere | 681 (8.1%) |
| **With a conflict in task files** | **44 (0.52%)** |
| **Repositories where this happened** | **20 of 130 = 15.4%** |
## Verdict against the thresholds set before the start
| Threshold | Condition | Result |
| Confirmed | > 30% of repositories | no |
| Refuted | < 10% | no |
**The hypothesis is neither confirmed nor refuted.** The value landed in the middle zone, closer to the lower bound. By the probe plan this means moving on to [Probe B](DOC-49).
## What this means without dressing it up
**The problem exists, but it is rare.** A conflict in task files happens in roughly one merge in two hundred. A team doing 20 merges a month meets one once every five months.

The objection from the "PM devil's advocate" in the [assumptions map](DOC-39) was borne out: the problem is real, but not daily. A product that brilliantly solves an event that happens once every five months is hard to sell against a tool people use every day.

**The distribution is extremely uneven.** In 110 of the 130 repositories — not a single conflict. But in `usmcamp0811/crystal-forge` there are 7, in `jpoley/flowspec` and `yaleh/baime` — 5 each. That is, there is a minority of teams for whom this is a genuine, regular pain. It is a narrower segment than the PRD assumed, but it is real and it can be found by name — which directly closes the gap "zero named early adopters" from the [Lean Canvas](DOC-26).
## The main finding: the type of conflicts
A classification of 28 conflicts from the six most active repositories:
| Type | Count | What it means | Does append-only eliminate it |
| **`CONFLICT (content)`** | **25 (89%)** | Two branches **edited the same task** | **Yes** — exactly the scenario of our spike |
| `CONFLICT (add/add)` | 2 (7%) | Two branches created tasks with the **same ID** | **No, not automatically** |
| `CONFLICT (modify/delete)` | 1 (4%) | One branch edited, the other deleted | Yes |
**This is the most valuable result of the probe.** The overwhelming majority of real conflicts are exactly the type our architecture eliminates by construction. The mechanism hits its target.

> An intermediate observation on a single repository (`InbarR/tmax`) showed add/add dominating and led to the opposite conclusion. A wider sample refuted it — which is why the report keeps the classification across six repositories rather than across one.
## A hole in our own specification that the probe exposed
`add/add` is an identifier collision: two branches independently created a task with the same number. That is exactly what the open task `task-4.12` in the Backlog.md backlog is about.

**Our current design does not solve this problem.** In [SPEC.md](../../SPEC.md), module M5, it is written: "IDs are issued sequentially and derived from the journal". But two branches that diverged from a common ancestor see the **same** journal — and both will derive `KAD-42`. There will be no file merge conflict (the events lie in separate files), but two different tasks with one number will appear, and that is worse than a conflict: the error is silent.

**The fix:** the primary identifier of a task is a ULID, globally unique by construction. The human-readable `KAD-42` becomes a **derived label**, assigned deterministically while folding the journal, by ULID order. Then the two branches will create tasks with different ULIDs, and after the merge they will automatically get the numbers 42 and 43.
This makes us the only tool in the category that closes **both** types of conflict.
## Effect on decisions
1. **Not refuted — the code is not blocked.** But also not confirmed enough to build the positioning around conflicts as the main message.
2. **The positioning on velocity** ([positioning.md](DOC-29)) gains support: conflicts are too rare to be the main selling argument.
3. **The M5 correction has to go into SPEC before the code starts** — it concerns the data model, not the implementation.
4. **A list of real interview candidates has appeared.** The 20 repositories where this actually happened are exactly the people it makes sense to talk to in Probe B.
## Limitations
- Merge commits show only **explicit** merges. Work through `rebase` or squash-merge does not enter these statistics, so the real frequency may be higher.
- The limit of 300 merges per repository understates the measure for the most active projects.
- The classification of types was done on 6 repositories out of 20, not on all of them.
- The sample is public repositories. Private team repositories, where there is more parallel work, are inaccessible and could give a different picture.
